text: The claims agree that agent work has shifted toward agentic, terminal-based settings in which agents act directly on repositories and build systems, and that trajectory analysis is an emerging way to understand them.

Trace representations vary by purpose. One line normalizes logs into thought-action-result triples (120 trajectories), another releases trajectories and execution traces as open artifacts, and an observability taxonomy defines explicit task status fields.

Persistence is framed as a design choice among append-only logs, structured databases, checkpoint snapshots, and stateless designs, and the one harness analyzed in detail is reported to implement append-only durable state.

On vector storage the claims pull apart. One harness analysis says memory retrieval uses no embeddings or vector index, and relies on an LLM scan of file headers. A software-engineering survey reports that DroidAgent stores embedded history in an external embedding database.

The Claude Code analysis characterises retrieval-augmented approaches as gaining flexibility at the cost of inspectability, and it notes that Claude Code avoids embeddings for memory retrieval and keeps CLAUDE.md as plain-text Markdown. Together these suggest that, in this analysis, the choice of storage affects how inspectable stored memory is. The claims do not directly show how this affects the minability of traces.
Other approaches also appear: coordination records kept as a signed append-only event log inside git, and an event-sourcing design whose overhead is reported negligible in production data.

Observability standards are described as incomplete for agents, since OpenTelemetry conventions leave some orchestration phases without span representation and provenance work says agents add objects existing traditions do not capture.

The claims show that traces are represented in several ways, including thought-action-result triples, released trajectories and execution traces, append-only logs, and event logs in git. Task state is explicit in at least one observability taxonomy.

The claims give no evidence that vector databases are the dominant way to store or mine traces. The single vector-database example concerns a survey-reported agent's history, and one harness is reported to avoid embeddings.

The claims do not allow a side-by-side comparison of logging granularity across SWE-agent, OpenHands, Claude Code, Aider, and Codex CLI. Aider is not covered at all. Codex CLI appears only as a terminal coding-assistant description and as an example of a terminal-based product, with no trace-format details.
